## Cumulative distribution functions \[DS 3.3\] \[Lec 8\] {#sec:cumul-distr-funct}

So far we've made a clear distinction between continuous RVs (for which
pdfs are the probability density) and discrete RVs (for which pmfs are
the density).

We now introduce one concept -- cumulative distribution functions (cdfs)
-- that can serve as general-purpose descriptions of
distributions/random variables.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**Cumulative Distribution Function.**

For all $x\in \bR$, the cumulative distribution function $F$ is the
function $$F(x) = \mathbb{P}(X \le x).$$
:::

discrete continuous random variables $X$ can be defined using a cdf.

Suppose $X$ has pmf $f(\cdot)$, then its cdf is:
$$F(x) = \sum\nolimits_{y \le x} f(y).$$

Also, suppose $X$ has pdf $f(\cdot)$, then its cdf is:
$$F(x) = \int\nolimits_{-\infty}^x f(y)dy.$$

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
Find and sketch the cdfs of the following random variables.

-   Bernoulli($p$).

-   Uniform distribution on $[0,1]$.
:::

Conversely, $f(x) = \frac{d}{dx}F(x)$ at all $x$ where $F$ is
differentiable.

(note the resemblance to the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.)

(Also note that sometimes we will include the subscript $X$ in cdfs
($F_X$) or pdfs or pmfs ($f_X$).)

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
Find the pdf of the following cdf:
$$F(x)= \begin{cases}0 & \text { for } x<0 \\ x^{2 / 3} & \text { for } 0 \leq x \leq 1 \\ 1 & \text { for } x>1\end{cases}$$

(Hint: draw the cdf. What are all the differentiable points?)
:::

Next, here are some properties of cdfs:

-   \(1\) A cdf is non-decreasing: $F(x_1) \le F(x_2)$ if $x_1<x_2$.

-   \(2\) A cdf's limits are at $\pm \infty$.

-   \(3\) A cdf is always continuous from the right: $F(x) =F(x^+)$ for
    all $x \in \bR$.

Here we pause and emphasize that a cdf need not be continuous. In fact,
the value of $F(x)$ may jump at any finite or countable number of
points.

You can calculate probabilities regarding random variable $X$ directly
from its cdf $F$ in the following ways:

-   \(1\) For every $x \in \bR$, $\mathbb{P}(X>x) = 1- F(x)$.

-   \(2\) For all $x_1<x_2$,
    $\mathbb{P}( x_1 <X \le x_2) = F(x_2) - F(x_1)$.

-   \(3\) For every $x \in \bR$, $\mathbb{P}(X<x) = F(x^-)$.

-   \(4\) For every $x \in \bR$, $\mathbb{P}(X=x) = F(x) - F(x^-)$.

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
Take a random variable $X$ whose cdf $F$ is as follows. [^1]

![image](cdf-ds-fig-3.9.png){width=".65\\linewidth"}
:::

What are these probabilities? (We will do only a few in class.)

::: multicols
2

-   $\mathbb{P}(X=-1)$

-   $\mathbb{P}(X<0)$

-   $\mathbb{P}(X \leq 0)$

-   $\mathbb{P}(X=1)$

-   $\mathbb{P}(0<X \leq 3)$

-   $\mathbb{P}(0<X<3)$

-   $\mathbb{P}(0 \leq X \leq 3)$

-   $\mathbb{P}(1<X \leq 2)$

-   $\mathbb{P}(1 \leq X \leq 2)$

-   $\mathbb{P}(X>5)$

-   $\mathbb{P}(X \geq 5)$

-   $\mathbb{P}(3 \leq X \leq 4)$
:::
:::

Next, we learn about an alternative representation of a random
variable's distribution, the *quantile* function. A quantile function is
*roughly* the inverse of the cdf.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**Quantile.**

For $p \in (0,1)$, $p-$quantile of $X$, denoted as $F^{-1}(p)$, is the
smallest value $x$ such that $$F(x) \ge p.$$ a.k.a. $100p$ percentile of
$X$
:::

**median.**

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
Sketch is the quantile function of $X\sim \text{Binom}(2,0.5)$.
:::

One might ask: when is a quantile an exact inverse of a cdf?

::: {.callout-important title="Theorem"}
When the random variable $X$ is continuous, the quantile function
$F^{-1}$ is the inverse of $F$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
Find the quantile functions for the following distributions.

-   Uniform on $[0,1]$.

-   Exponential distribution: $f(x) = 2e^{-2x}$ for $x>0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**Frequently used quantiles.**

The 1/2 quantile or the 50th percentile of a distribution is called its
*median*. The 1/4 quantile or 25th percentile is the lower *quartile*.
The 3/4 quantile or 75th percentile is called the upper quartile.
:::

The median is the number divides the distribution in half as closely as
is possible.

(And if there are ties, take the middle value).

A median of a distribution is important because it helps *summarize* the
distribution of a random variable, answering the question: what is the
most "representative" value?

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
What are the medians of the following random variables?

-   $X\sim \text{Unif}(0,10)$? (What is the upper quartile?)

-   $X\sim \text{N}(0,1)$?

-   $X\sim \text{Binom}(5,0.5)$?
:::

(There are other summaries of *central tendency*, like "what is the
center of gravity?" (mean) or "what is the most frequent value?" (mode).
We will learn more about these soon.)
